title: Linux and the Command Line for Support
subtitle: Navigate, inspect, and grab evidence fast
description: Nearly every SaaS server runs Linux. Learn the shell commands support engineers use every day to navigate a box, read its logs, check its resources, and prove what happened.

lessons.title: The Shell and Navigation
lessons.body:
The **shell** is a text program that reads the commands you type and runs them for the operating system. Bash is the most common shell. When you see a prompt like `ubuntu@web-01:~$`, the part before the `@` is your user, the part after it is the machine, and the symbol at the end shows your **privileges**: `$` for a normal user, `#` for root, the all-powerful administrator account.

Every file on Linux sits in one giant tree that starts at `/`, the **root directory**. A path is simply the route to a file: `/var/log/nginx/error.log` walks down from the top. Paths starting with `/` are **absolute** (always complete), while paths that do not are **relative** (resolved from where you are standing right now).

Four commands move you around:

```
pwd             # where am I? (print working directory)
ls              # what is here?
ls -la          # everything, including hidden files, with details
cd /var/log     # go there; cd ~ returns home, cd .. goes up one level
```

Files whose names start with a dot are hidden, so `ls -la` is how you see them.

exercises.prompt: Which command prints the full path of the directory you are currently in?
exercises.explain: pwd stands for print working directory, and that is exactly what it prints.
exercises.hint: Its name is three words long, initials only.

exercises.prompt: You are at the prompt `ubuntu@web-01:~$`. What does the `~` mean?
exercises.explain: The tilde is shorthand for your home directory, and `cd ~` always takes you back there.
exercises.hint: It is the one place that belongs to you, whatever your username is.

exercises.prompt: Write the exact `ls` command that shows the current directory in long format (permissions and sizes) including hidden files — both flags required
exercises.hint: Two single-letter flags combined: -l for long format, -a for all files.
exercises.explain: ls -la lists everything with details; without -a you never see the dotfiles.

lessons.title: Reading Files
lessons.body:
`cat` prints a whole file to the screen at once. That is fine for a small config file and a disaster for a 2 GB log, because your terminal has to load everything and you scroll straight past the part you needed. For big files, reach for `less` instead:

```
less /var/log/syslog
```

Inside `less` you move with the arrow keys or space bar, search by typing `/pattern`, and quit with `q`. It only loads what fits on screen.

`head` and `tail` read the two ends of a file: `head -n 50 app.log` shows the first 50 lines (handy for learning the log's format), and `tail -n 100 app.log` shows the last 100 lines (handy for what just happened). The `tail -f` variant is the support engineer's best friend: it prints new lines as they are written, so you can watch a live log while you reproduce the customer's issue:

```
tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log
```

Press `Ctrl+C` to stop watching.

exercises.prompt: A customer sends you a 3 GB log file. Which tool should you open it with?
options: less, because it only loads what fits on screen
cat, because it shows everything at once
echo, because it is the fastest command
cd, because you need to enter the file first
exercises.explain: less reads a huge file lazily, so your terminal stays responsive and you can search inside it.
exercises.hint: One of these commands was built for paging through large files interactively.

exercises.prompt: Write the exact command that watches `app.log` live, printing each new line as it is written
exercises.hint: tail with the flag that means follow.
exercises.explain: tail -f keeps the file open and echoes new lines, which is how you watch a request arrive in real time.

exercises.prompt: Write the exact command that prints the last 100 lines of `app.log`
exercises.hint: tail plus the line-count flag, then the number, then the file.
exercises.explain: tail -n 100 app.log prints the final 100 lines, which is usually where the current problem lives.

exercises.prompt: You have never seen this log file before. Put the steps in order, from your first look to watching it live
items: Check the file's size and location with ls -lh app.log
Look at the first 50 lines with head -n 50 to learn the format
Read it interactively with less, searching with /pattern
Follow it live with tail -f while reproducing the issue
exercises.explain: Size first, then format, then browse, then follow: know what you are looking at before you watch it.
exercises.hint: Start broad and static, finish narrow and live.

lessons.title: Searching and Filtering
lessons.body:
`grep` hunts for text inside files. The three flags you will actually use: `-i` ignores upper or lower case, `-n` shows line numbers, and `-r` searches every file under a directory tree.

```
grep -i error app.log              # any line containing 'error', any case
grep -n "17:42:05" app.log         # matching lines, with their numbers
grep -r "TimeoutException" /var/log/
```

The **pipe**, written `|`, feeds the output of one command into the next, so you can build small pipelines. Three commands finish most of them: `wc -l` counts lines, `sort` puts lines in order, and `uniq` collapses neighbouring duplicates (which is why you sort first):

```
grep -i error app.log | wc -l                       # how many errors?
grep -i error app.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn    # which error, how often?
```

That second line is a real support reflex. When a customer says the log is full of errors, the questions are which error and how many. Quote any pattern containing spaces, like `grep "connection refused" app.log`, so the shell passes it through as one argument.

exercises.prompt: What does the pipe character `|` do?
options: Sends the output of one command into the next command
Copies a file to a new location
Runs two commands at the same time
Stops the command you are running
exercises.explain: A pipe chains commands together: what comes out of the left side becomes the input on the right.
exercises.hint: It is how you build a mini one-line program.

exercises.prompt: Write the exact command that searches `app.log` for the word `error` ignoring case (so ERROR and Error both match)
exercises.hint: grep, then the ignore-case flag, then the word and the file.
exercises.explain: The -i flag makes grep match error, Error and ERROR alike, which is what you want when formats vary.

exercises.prompt: Write the exact command that counts how many lines in `app.log` contain `error`, ignoring case
exercises.hint: grep for the lines first, then pipe them into the line-count command.
exercises.explain: grep filters the lines and wc -l counts them, giving you one number to compare against a minute ago.

exercises.prompt: Put this pipeline in the order the data actually flows, from the log file to a ranked report
items: grep -i error app.log   (keep only the error lines)
exercises.explain: Filter, then group, then count, then rank: that order is what makes the report readable.
exercises.hint: You cannot count duplicates until they are sitting next to each other.

lessons.title: Processes and Resources
lessons.body:
A **process** is any program currently running, and each one has a **PID** (process ID). `ps aux` prints a snapshot of them all: user, PID, CPU and memory use, and the command. For a live view use `top` (or `htop`, a friendlier version) — press `q` to quit.

When a process misbehaves, `kill PID` asks it politely to stop (the normal **SIGTERM** signal). If it ignores you, `kill -9 PID` forces it down (**SIGKILL**). Always try the polite form first, so the service can close files and finish requests cleanly.

Two checks solve most of the tickets that start with 'the server is slow':

```
df -h       # disk free, human-readable sizes — watch Use% on /var
free -m     # memory in megabytes
uptime      # load average over 1, 5 and 15 minutes
```

**Saturation** means a resource has hit its limit. A disk at 100% makes every write fail (logs stop, databases crash), and a process pinned near 100% CPU for minutes is a runaway — that is the PID you find in `top` and kill.

options: Forces process 4821 to stop immediately, with no chance to clean up
Waits for process 4821 to finish on its own
exercises.explain: -9 is SIGKILL: it cannot be ignored, so use plain kill first and escalate only if the process refuses.
exercises.hint: The 9 makes it a demand, not a request.

exercises.prompt: Write the exact command that shows how full each disk partition is, with human-readable sizes
exercises.explain: df -h reports capacity and Use% per mount point — the fastest way to spot a full disk.

exercises.prompt: Write the exact command that prints a snapshot of the running processes with user, PID, CPU and memory
exercises.hint: Two letters, then three classic flags: a, u, x.
exercises.explain: ps aux is the standard process listing you will see in every interview and on every box.

exercises.prompt: A web app has stopped responding. Put these triage steps in order, from the broad health check to taking action
items: Check the overall load with uptime and glance at top
Confirm disk and memory with df -h and free -m
Pinpoint the stuck process with ps aux
Stop it with kill PID, escalating to kill -9 PID only if it refuses
exercises.explain: Broad to specific: see whether the box is overloaded, rule resources in or out, identify the process, then act on it.
exercises.hint: Never kill anything before you know which PID and why.

lessons.title: Permissions, Services, and Networking
lessons.body:
Linux tracks **users** and **groups**, and every file carries an owner, a group, and three permissions (read, write, execute) for each of them. `ls -l` shows the result as something like `rwxr-xr-x`. Two commands change it: `chmod` changes the mode (the permissions), `chown` changes the owner.

```
chmod 640 app.conf       # owner reads/writes, group reads, others nothing
chown app:app app.conf   # hand the file to the app user and group
```

On a production box you are rarely root (the superuser). `sudo systemctl restart nginx` runs a single command as root, and it is logged. **systemd** is the service manager: `systemctl status nginx` tells you whether the service is `active (running)` or `failed`, and `systemctl restart nginx` bounces it.

To check whether something is listening or reachable:

```
curl -I https://example.com   # ask a URL for its headers
ss -tulpn                     # listening ports and the process on them
```

A quick support loop: `systemctl status` for the service, `ss -tulpn` for the port, `curl` from the client side.

exercises.prompt: Which command changes who owns a file?
exercises.explain: chown is change owner; chmod changes the permissions on the file instead.
exercises.hint: The second half of the command name is 'own'.

exercises.prompt: Write the exact systemctl command that shows whether the `nginx` service is running
exercises.hint: systemctl, then the subcommand that reports state, then the service name.
exercises.explain: systemctl status nginx shows active (running), failed, or stopped, plus the last few log lines.

exercises.prompt: Write the exact `ss` command that shows all listening TCP and UDP sockets with the process using them and without DNS lookups (five single-letter flags: t, u, l, p, n)
exercises.hint: ss followed by one flag combining t, u, l, p and n.
exercises.explain: ss -tulpn answers 'is anything listening on 8080, and which process owns it?' (netstat is the older command for the same job).

exercises.prompt: A customer reports the app is down. Put these checks in order, working from inside the server outwards
items: systemctl status app — is the service active?
ss -tulpn — is the app listening on its port?
curl -I http://localhost:8080 — does it answer on the box itself?
curl -I https://app.example.com — does it answer from outside?
exercises.explain: Inside out: service, then port, then local HTTP, then the outside view — each step narrows where the fault is.
exercises.hint: Start with the process and finish with what the customer sees.
